justification: Canonical equals brute force on all 1,006 inputs and the docstring is unambiguous, but the base set never exercises an equal-gap pair, so right-core programs with an inclusive comparison pass base and fail exactly the six exact-gap plus inputs — 262 attempts, 114 and 46 in single arms, far above the bar; one nameable task-defined boundary mishandled by otherwise-correct programs.

justification: Prompt, canonical (verified against exact rational arithmetic on all 974 inputs) and tests agree and every plus input is an in-domain positive finite float, but the unexercised input 4.999999999999999 (fractional part 0.9999999999999991) fells 20/128 gpt-5-mini and 3/128 gpt-5-nano texts whose core (number - floor / modf) is right and which only added a peripheral 'snap noise within 1e-12 of 1 to 0.0' rule. The remaining failures are example-exercised base errors (number - round, modf order, str digits without '0.'), emission slips, and a wrong-core string-repr model crashing on the denormals 1e-323/3e-323 (deepseek-coder-33b 6) - capability, not defects.
label: tricky

justification: Task is self-consistent (canonical reproduces the docstring example and all base tests), but the plus tests exercise the empty string, expecting [] — so `split(' ')` (yielding [''] -> [0]) fails while idiomatic `split()`/empty-token filtering passes. A second gotcha: depth is per space-separated token, not per balanced group, so '(())(()())' is one group -> [2].
label: tricky

justification: The only label-bearing mechanism is the empty list: 336 attempts (294 distinct right-core running-max texts) pass all 959 plus inputs and the 3 non-empty base inputs and die only on base[0] = [] with IndexError from seeding numbers[0] — an unexercised boundary of the right model (the docstring example is non-empty, the prose never mentions emptiness, and [] -> [] is the only reasonable answer) with victims >= 5 in ten arms (deepseek-coder-1.3b 77/128, Qwen2.5-3B 51, Moonlight 42, Coder-0.5B 34, Qwen2.5-0.5B 34, Coder-1.5B 26, deepseek-coder-6.7b 21, Qwen3-0.6B-think 19, Qwen2.5-1.5B 17, Qwen3-0.6B 8; 4.6% of all attempts). The negative-seed slip (0/-1 sentinel, 18 attempts, only Qwen2.5-0.5B 14 at the bar) mis-answers every list whose first element is negative (455/959 plus rows, 446 of them mixed-sign) and is read core-side/regular; all other failures are wrong cores that fail the docstring example itself or emission slips.
label: tricky

justification: Self-consistent and solvable by the plain minimal reading (canonical passes 408/408; 21/22 arms >=90%), but the lone docstring example is silent on the convention 332/408 graded inputs enforce, so solvers importing binary-number semantics (lstrip/int()/(''->'0')) fail — the technically-underspecified-but-intent-obvious bucket.
label: tricky

justification: The prompt is unambiguous (a str 'consists of' all its characters; 'regardless of case' is a case-fold instruction, not a letters filter) and the canonical is correct, but both docstring examples are letters-only, so letters-only/space-stripping programs (isalpha/isalnum/replace(' ','')) fit both examples and are felled by hidden BASE input 'Jerry jERRY JeRRRY' (expected 5, they return 4): 132 example-correct attempts, >=5 in 7 arms (Qwen2.5-3B 43, deepseek-coder-6.7b 36, Moonlight-16B 16, Qwen2.5-1.5B 10, Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B 7, Qwen3-32B 7, Qwen2.5-0.5B 5), 1.8% of all attempts. The other failure mass (137 attempts ignoring the explicit 'regardless of case' or not deduplicating) fails the docstring's own first example and is plain capability; nothing is grader-side or label-bearing beyond the trap.
label: tricky

justification: Prompt, example, and canonical solution agree exactly, but two gotchas bite: the tested input '' requires [] while a natural `split(" ")` yields ['']->[None] (12 samples failed), and 'o' vs 'o|' needs exact-token matching, so substring checks like `'o' in note` mis-score half notes (56 samples failed on 'o o| o| o|'). Both behaviors are inferable from the legend and example, so this is a fair-but-subtle task rather than a spec defect.
label: tricky

justification: Prompt, example and canonical solution agree ('three one five' -> 'one three five'), but the base tests exercise the unmentioned empty-string input, where the literal "space-delimited" reading `numbers.split(" ")` raises KeyError — the canonical solution needs an explicit `if numbers == "": return ""` guard. Duplicate-preserving stable output is likewise only implicit, though both intended behaviors are obvious.
label: tricky

justification: Tie-breaking among equally-close pairs is never shown: both docstring examples and all 5 base tests have a unique minimum gap, yet the plus input [1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5] (all gaps 1.0) pins the leftmost pair (1.5, 2.5), so a `<=` update rule silently fails. The gotcha is subtle but the required behavior is what the natural strict-`<` scan-adjacent-in-sorted-order implementation already produces.
label: tricky

justification: The plus tests exercise booleans (input [True, False, None, 0, -10, 'test', [], {}, 3.14] expects [0, -10]), requiring bools be excluded because the canonical solution uses `type(x) == int`, but the docstring and both examples contain no boolean and give no way to infer this. Since `bool` subclasses `int` in Python, the idiomatic `isinstance(x, int)` reading is the opposite, and it failed all 384 samples despite passing every base test.
label: underspecification

justification: Three graded plus inputs admit NO float64 return value satisfying the |poly(xs,x)|<=1e-4 oracle (best achievable residual ~2.3e-3, independently reproduced), and the canonical solution itself fails 7 graded plus inputs on the eval platform's libm — the plus test set is unpassable by any solution, contradicting the ground truth.
label: contradiction

justification: "Three distinct elements" actually means three distinct indices, not distinct values, and the plus tests exercise this ([0, 0, 0] and [1, 1, -2, -2] both expect True). The prompt's own example [1, 3, -2, 1] -> True already resolves the ambiguity, so it is a subtle gotcha rather than a real gap; all docstring examples agree with the canonical solution.
label: tricky

justification: "Two distinct elements" is genuinely ambiguous between distinct indices and distinct values, and the docstring examples never disambiguate; tests grade pairs_sum_to_zero([0,0])==True, pinning the indices reading arbitrarily.
label: underspecification

justification: The only failing plus input is x=0 (not covered by any docstring example), where the naive `while x > 0` loop returns '' instead of the canonical '0' — the classic zero-case gotcha in base conversion. Intent is still reasonably inferable, since '0' is the only sensible string representation of zero in any base, so this is a fair subtle trap rather than a spec gap.
label: tricky

justification: The docstring example claims median([-10, 4, 6, 1000, 10, 20]) == 15.0, but the canonical solution returns 8.0 (sorted middle pair 6 and 10), so it fails its own documented example. The base test enforces the canonical value with assert candidate([-10, 4, 6, 1000, 10, 20]) == 8.0, directly contradicting the prompt.
label: contradiction

justification: All examples are lowercase and space-free, so they never show whether spaces/case are normalized, yet plus tests use famous phrase palindromes ('never odd or even', 'Rats live on no evil star') that must return False — punishing the common "helpful" strip-spaces/lowercase implementation. The plain reading ("the given string is a palindrome", i.e. text == reversed text) is still the standard default and matches every example, so it is solvable, just a gotcha.
label: tricky

justification: Canonical is exactly pow(2, n, p) and all docstring examples hold, but the tests exercise p=1 (modp(0,1)==0, 168 sample failures), so implementations that special-case n==0 as 1 or skip the final `% p` break; the docstring's modp(0,101)==1 invites that mistake. Composite moduli like p=20 are also tested, defeating Fermat-style exponent reduction that the prime-only examples suggest.
label: tricky

justification: The docstring declares decode_shift's input as a string produced by encode_shift, whose image is exactly a-z, yet 479/1000 plus inputs contain spaces, digits or non-ASCII letters and the tests demand the canonical's blind-formula output on them (' '->'i', '0'->'y'), which decodes nothing (decode(encode(' '))='n'). 476 attempts (6.5% of 7326; >=5 in 16 arms, 73/128 in Qwen2.5-14B, 53/128 in gpt-5-nano, 22/128 in DeepSeek-V3-0324) pass every in-domain input (100/100 base, 521/521 in-domain plus) and fail only on those out-of-domain inputs - class note 2a, an explicit input guarantee contradicted by the tests, not capability.
label: contradiction

justification: The prose never says vowel removal is case-insensitive or that 'y' is excluded, yet tests exercise both ('EcBOO'->'cB', 'AEIOUaeiouq'->'q', 'ybcd'->'ybcd'); the docstring example remove_vowels('aaBAA')->'B' makes the uppercase intent obvious, so it is only a missable gotcha, not a real gap.
label: tricky

justification: The three examples (fib(1)=1, fib(8)=21, fib(10)=55) pin the standard indexing exactly, so the plus-tested fib(0)=0 is obvious even though it is not shown; the real gotchas are that off-by-one indexings pass nothing and that n=63 (6557470319842) times out any naive exponential recursion, which the docstring never hints at.
label: tricky

justification: Prompt and canonical solution are fully consistent (all three docstring examples pass), but the tests hinge on non-strict monotonicity — equal adjacent elements count as monotonic ([4,1,1,0], [9,9,9,9], [1,1,1,1,1] -> True) — and no docstring example contains a tie, so most failures come from readers assuming strict increase/decrease. The standard reading of "monotonically increasing" (vs. "strictly") makes the intended weak comparison derivable, so this is a subtle gotcha rather than a defect.
label: tricky

justification: The tests pin an output-representation convention the docstring and examples never touch: the zero derivative must be [] for [1]/[0] yet keep trailing zeros for inputs like [1,0,0,0,0,0,0] — a pin not derivable from the prompt.
label: underspecification

justification: Consistent and derivable, but with subtle traps the tests exercise: the empty string (tested, expected 0) makes the natural `s[-1]` check raise IndexError, and only the final 'y'/'Y' counts, so "aeiouyaeiouy" is 11 (interior y ignored) while a mid-word y in "bye" adds nothing. Uppercase handling is pinned by the "ACEDY" -> 3 example, so intent is clear.
label: tricky

justification: The boundary shift == number of digits is a full rotation returning the digits unchanged rather than the reversal used for shift > digits, and shift > digits reverses instead of shifting by shift % len (1234,6 -> "4321", not "3412"); models that wrote `shift >= len` fail input [12,2], but the docstring's own example circular_shift(12, 2) == "12" pins that down, so the spec and tests are fully consistent.
label: tricky

justification: The Constraints block says "1 <= nodes.length" yet Example 3 and the base tests pass [], so a reader trusting the constraint could skip the empty-array guard — but the prose ("or the given array is empty, return []") and Example 3 make the intent obvious. Other traps (smallest even vs. first even, 0 being even, returning [] instead of a sentinel like [inf,-1]) are all explicitly stated in the docstring.
label: tricky

justification: All three docstring examples are even-length or empty, yet the tests heavily exercise odd-length lists (e.g. [5, 6, 7, 8, 9] -> [5, 9, 6, 8, 7]), where the naive min/max-pair loop emits the middle element twice. The behavior is fully derivable from "minimum, then maximum of the remaining" (canonical solution matches that literal reading on every tested input, duplicates included), so it is a gotcha rather than a spec gap.
label: tricky

justification: All four docstring examples match the canonical solution `q == q[::-1] and sum(q) <= w`, so the spec is self-consistent; the only gotcha is the untested-by-example empty list, where the plus tests require `will_it_fly([], 0) == True` and a natural `if not q: return False` guard fails. That behavior still follows directly from the stated rules ([] is palindromic, sum 0 <= 0), so it is a subtle trap rather than a specification gap.
label: tricky

justification: Fully consistent (all 5 docstring examples and every tested input match the canonical `c1 <= c2` rule), but the tie case is only demonstrated by the degenerate `([], [])` example, so the stated "same number of chars → first list" rule is easy to drop — it caused the two largest failure clusters (7-vs-7 and 18-vs-18 inputs). Secondary gotchas: an empty list is not special-cased (`(['this'], []) -> []`), and the name `total_match` plus case-varied strings like 'hI'/'Hi' are red herrings suggesting case-insensitive matching.
label: tricky

justification: The tests count prime factors with multiplicity (8=2*2*2 and 99=3*3*11 are True, 90=2*3*3*5 is False), while the docstring's only example uses three distinct primes — a fair but easily missed reading of "multiplication of 3 prime numbers", and the source of nearly all failures. Negative/zero inputs like -98 and 0 are also tested (the contract only bounds a < 100), but False is the obvious inference since no product of primes is non-positive.
label: tricky

justification: The plus suite exercises undefined edges the docstring/examples never touch — above all is_simple_power(1,0), whose expected True rests solely on Python's 0**0==1 convention (math: indeterminate) and on the canonical happening to check x==1 before n==0; 69/128 Qwen3-32B samples are perfect on all 906 other inputs and fail only there (8/128 -> 77/128 plus if that one input is dropped). Traces are overwhelmingly pattern (a): 128/128 call 0^0 undefined, 102/128 call the spec ambiguous, and 92/93 (1,0)-failers deliberately conclude "returns False. Correct.".
label: underspecification

justification: The docstring guarantees the input is "a hexadecimal number as a string ... always correct or empty string", but the tests pass non-string inputs `[]` (base) and `{}` (plus) and require 0, which only works via `filter`'s duck typing. This explicitly-ruled-out behavior is the dominant failure mode (20 samples failed on `[]`, 20 on `{}`, e.g. a string-faithful `num.upper()` raising AttributeError).
label: contradiction

justification: Tests exercise decimal=0 (expected "db0db"), which no example covers, but "0" is the conventional binary form so the intent is clear; the gotcha is that naive while-decimal>0 loops emit "dbdb" instead. The docstring's "each character will be '0' or '1'" is also loose given the 'db' wrapper, though the next sentence and examples resolve it.
label: tricky

justification: Prompt, canonical (== brute-force primality on n in 0..2000) and all 978 str inputs agree, so no defect label applies; the one peripheral, task-defined trap the four docstring examples (lengths 5,7,7,6) never exercise is the empty/one-character string (length 0 and 1 are not prime), which fells otherwise-correct trial-division programs whose n<2 guard is missing or written as ==1 in 55 attempts, clearing >=5 in five arms (Qwen2.5-0.5B@0.8 23, Qwen2.5-1.5B@0.8 7, deepseek-coder-33b@0.8 7, Qwen3-0.6B@0.8 6, Qwen3-0.6B-think 5). The larger plus-only collapse (Qwen3-0.6B@0.8 45) is a finite hardcoded prime table, i.e. a substituted core (regular-class), and the Qwen3-1.7B@0.8 15 are a wheel-6 bookkeeping slip (grader_class note).

justification: Spec, canonical solution and tests agree (canonical matches brute-force enumeration for n=1..6), but two gotchas bite: the leading-zero rule makes "ends with 1" 9*10^(n-2) not 10^(n-1), so careless inclusion-exclusion yields 19*10^(n-2) (19 for n=2, 198 for n=3), and the closed form needs an n==1 special case since 18*10**-1 is the float 1.8. The example-free docstring makes it hard, not ambiguous; the n=1000000 ValueError is a harness string-conversion artifact that any O(1) solution reproduces.

justification: The prompt and all four examples show only pure-lowercase inputs and never say what to do with other characters, yet 472/1000 plus inputs (0/8 base) contain digits/spaces/symbols whose pass-through-unchanged handling is pinned only by hidden tests. Qwen3-32B reads everything else perfectly (128/128 base, zero implementation errors) but its traces explicitly deliberate this exact open question and resolve it "assume letters only" in 120/128 samples — an undefined edge case massively exercised, with the same model family flipping sides non-monotonically across sizes (8B 119/128 vs 32B 8/128).

justification: "2nd smallest element" means 2nd smallest distinct value (duplicates collapse), which the docstring example next_smallest([1, 1]) == None makes explicit; the canonical solution matches every docstring example and base test. justification: The plus oracle pins the prompt-undefined edge is_bored("I")==0 (an artifact of the canonical's strip+startswith("I ") idiom), which no reasonable reading of "a sentence that starts with the word 'I'" yields: 102/128 Qwen3-32B traces explicitly derive the opposite, zero derive 0, and every faithful first-word solution across all six thinking models fails plus solely on that one input (plus 0/768). Base failures (letter-prefix startswith('I')) are genuine model errors against a clear spec, but the plus wipeout defining this task's low pass rate is a spec defect, not difficulty.

justification: Gotcha: the vowel substitute carries the swapped case ('test'->'TGST', 'TEST'->'tgst'), which most failing samples missed by emitting 'tGst'; the two docstring examples pin this down exactly, and the orders of the two operations provably commute so nothing is ambiguous. justification: Trap: the stated domain 'list of integers' admits negatives, 13 plus inputs carry them (e.g. plus 26 = [0,0,-1,2,5,7,11,13,17] -> 8) while all docstring examples are non-negative, and right-core programs (filter primes -> max -> digit sum) whose primality test omits the n<2 guard crash on sqrt of a negative (TypeError complex->int / ValueError math domain) only there. Victims clear the per-arm bar in two arms (deepseek-coder-1.3b@0.8 6/128, Qwen2.5-1.5B@0.8 5/128; 21 total across 6 arms), every other failure is a degenerate text, an example-failing wrong core, a size-class timeout or a below-bar slip.

justification: The prompt never defines caseless string keys, yet plus inputs like {'8':'banana'} and {'1':'apple','2':'banana','3':'cherry'} require False, arbitrarily pinning str.islower()/isupper() over the equally natural k == k.lower() reading (which matches every docstring example and every base test, but yields True here). The docstring's only non-alphabetic example uses the integer key 8, already covered by "keys are strings", so nothing resolves the digit-string case.

justification: Spec and examples are consistent (multiply(14,-15)==20 shows the sign is ignored, so unit digits are magnitudes), but Python's `%` gives the wrong digit for negatives (-9 % 10 == 1) and the only negative docstring example coincidentally passes with naive `a%10*b%10`. justification: "Even indices" is ambiguous (0-based vs 1-based) and the name count_upper suggests all uppercase letters, but the docstring examples pin both down: 'aBCdEf'==1 and 'dBBE'==0 are only satisfied by 0-based indices counting AEIOU only (1-based would give 0 and 1). justification: Tests grade the canonical solution's float64 parsing artifacts on 15 exercised 18-97-digit inputs, so the expected output contradicts the docstring's "closest integer" for integer-valued strings float64 cannot represent exactly.

justification: The canonical solution exactly matches a brute-force reading of the docstring for all contract-valid inputs (verified over x,y in 1..59), and both docstring examples pass. justification: Spec, examples, canonical solution and tests all agree (empty -> True is stated, duplicates are excluded by the contract, already-sorted -> True follows since N shifts are the identity). justification: Prompt/examples/canonical/tests all agree, but two gotchas bite: the documented `histogram('') == {}` case crashes naive `max()` code (87 sample failures), and a hidden plus input with a double space ('a b c  d e f g') penalizes `split(" ")` without filtering blanks — the intended "ignore blank tokens" behavior is obvious and `.split()` handles it.

justification: Two gotchas, both resolvable from the prompt: the result must be ascending-sorted (Example 1's [-4,-3,5] makes this explicit, yet most failures return descending order), and k=0 is allowed by Note 3 and tested (expects []), where the natural `arr[-k:]` idiom silently returns the whole array. justification: The docstring example only shows positive numbers, yet base and plus tests lean heavily on negatives, where digits are counted ignoring the minus sign (-99 included, -100 excluded) — the standard reading of "at most two digits" for an integer, but a gotcha models miss with guards like 0<=x<=99 or -100<=x<=99. justification: The only counting example, split_words("abcdef") == 3, is parity-symmetric (counting a,c,e also gives 3), so a reader must rely on the prompt's explicit 0-based mapping ("odd order", ord('a')=0) — tests like "aaabb" == 2 and "abc123" == 1 pin the b,d,f reading, which is derivable but easy to invert. justification: Docstring, examples (1→1, 4→0, 235→15) and canonical solution agree, and tests only probe the stated rule. The gotcha: a legitimate product of odd digits can equal 1 (tested inputs 120, 111), so the common `if product == 1: return 0` sentinel breaks — an explicit "has any odd digit" flag is required, and even digits must be skipped rather than multiplied in.

justification: Prompt, examples, canonical solution and tests all agree, but the "separated by space" definition must be taken literally: plus inputs like 'apple pi\ne' expect False (so txt.split() whitespace splitting fails) and 'muffin!A'/'1A' expect False since the preceding char must be a space, not merely a non-letter. justification: Prompt, both examples, and canonical solution fully agree (empty/singleton -> -1 follows from "if no such element exists"). The gotchas are only subtle wording: the double negative "not greater than or equal to" means strictly less than, and "largest index" demands a right-to-left scan returning the offending element's own index, while the sole example [1,2,4,3,5] has just one descent so it doesn't distinguish first-vs-last.

justification: Consistent: all four docstring examples match the canonical solution, and the tested edge cases (cross-type numeric equality like [10,'10.0'] -> None; returning the original object rather than the parsed float) are directly implied by the examples "1",1 -> None and 1,"2,3" -> "2,3". justification: Canonical matches all four docstring examples and every base test, but two gotchas bite: a run of exactly 2 spaces stays "__" (2 is not "more than 2"), and any run of 3+ spaces collapses to a single "-" regardless of length, so naive `.replace("   ", "-")` fails on 'Hey    there!'. justification: The docstring explicitly restricts the required leading letter to ("a"-"z" and "A"-"Z"), yet exercised plus inputs starting with "é" (outside that range) are graded "Yes" because the canonical uses isalpha() — the tests contradict the stated rule.

justification: Arguments may come in far-to-near order (tests use ("Earth","Mercury"), ("Neptune","Venus"), ("Neptune","Mercury")), so one must swap and still emit sun-ascending order — stated by "sorted by the proximity to the sun" plus example 2, but easy to miss; endpoints are also excluded and bad names must return () rather than raise. justification: The docstring states "You may assume that all words will have the same length," which is contradicted by its own examples (["aa","a","aaa"]) and by the tests (e.g. ['programming','python','java','ruby'] -> ['java','ruby','python']), and would make the prompt's own sort-by-length rule vacuous. justification: Prompt, examples, canonical solution and tests all agree, but tests exercise n <= 1 (base: n=1 -> y, n=2 -> x) and negative n (plus: -2, -3 -> y), which the standard definition of prime settles yet naive `all(n % i for i in range(2, int(n**0.5)+1))` checks get wrong or crash with a complex-sqrt TypeError.
